claim: In the Asia-Pacific region, there are more than 1.8 billion people at risk of infection with dengue viruses (DENV).
source: In the Asia-Pacific region, which bears 75% of the global dengue disease burden, there are more than 1.8 billion people at risk of infection with dengue viruses (DENV) (World Health Organization, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2009.

claim: The Asia-Pacific region bears 75% of the global dengue disease burden.
source: In the Asia-Pacific region, which bears 75% of the global dengue disease burden, there are more than 1.8 billion people at risk of infection with dengue viruses (DENV) (World Health Organization, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2009.

claim: Increased air travel and urbanisation could have contributed to the geographic spread of dengue infection.
source: Increased air travel and urbanisation could have contributed to the geographic spread of infection (Gubler, 1998; Simmons et al., 2012), with transmission by mosquitoes of the Aedes genus, including Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus (Halstead, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gubler, 1998 and Simmons et al., 2012.

claim: Dengue is transmitted by mosquitoes of the Aedes genus, including Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus.
source: Increased air travel and urbanisation could have contributed to the geographic spread of infection (Gubler, 1998; Simmons et al., 2012), with transmission by mosquitoes of the Aedes genus, including Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus (Halstead, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Halstead, 2007.

claim: DENV has four serotypes circulating.
source: DENV has four serotypes circulating, with infection conferring lifelong protection against the infecting serotype and short-lived protection against the others (Sabin, 1952; Guzmán and Kourí, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sabin, 1952 and Guzmán and Kourí, 2002.

claim: DENV infection confers lifelong protection against the infecting serotype and short-lived protection against the others.
source: DENV has four serotypes circulating, with infection conferring lifelong protection against the infecting serotype and short-lived protection against the others (Sabin, 1952; Guzmán and Kourí, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sabin, 1952 and Guzmán and Kourí, 2002.

claim: Four serotypes of DENV may co-circulate in South East Asia.
source: Although four serotypes of DENV may co-circulate in South East Asia, only one serotype circulates in most of the South Pacific islands at any point in time (Cao-Lormeau et al., 2014; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cao-Lormeau et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2010.

claim: Only one DENV serotype circulates in most of the South Pacific islands at any point in time.
source: Although four serotypes of DENV may co-circulate in South East Asia, only one serotype circulates in most of the South Pacific islands at any point in time (Cao-Lormeau et al., 2014; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cao-Lormeau et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2010.

claim: Between November 2013 and July 2014, a major outbreak caused by DENV-3 occurred in Fiji, with more than 25,000 suspected cases reported.
source: Between November 2013 and July 2014, a major outbreak caused by DENV-3 occurred in Fiji, with more than 25,000 suspected cases reported (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Prior to the 2013/14 outbreak, there were eleven outbreaks of dengue recorded in Fiji, involving serotypes 1, 2 and 4.
source: Prior to the 2013/14 outbreak, there were eleven outbreaks of dengue recorded in Fiji, involving serotypes 1, 2 and 4 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by historical outbreak data presented in Table 1.

claim: Most cases in 2013/14 occurred on Viti Levu, the largest and most populous island.
source: Most cases in 2013/14 occurred on Viti Levu, the largest and most populous island.
evidence: The claim is based on surveillance data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dengue transmission in Central and Western Divisions is likely to be driven mostly by the Aedes aegypti vector.
source: Dengue transmission in Central and Western Divisions is likely to be driven mostly by the Aedes aegypti vector, with Aedes albopictus most abundant in the Northern Division.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known vector distributions.

claim: Aedes albopictus is most abundant in the Northern Division of Fiji.
source: Dengue transmission in Central and Western Divisions is likely to be driven mostly by the Aedes aegypti vector, with Aedes albopictus most abundant in the Northern Division.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known vector distributions.

claim: Aedes polynesiensis and Aedes pseudoscutellaris are present in all divisions of Fiji.
source: Aedes polynesiensis and Aedes pseudoscutellaris are also present in all divisions (Maguire et al., 1971; Prakash et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maguire et al., 1971 and Prakash et al., 2001.

claim: A nationwide vector clean-up campaign was conducted between 8th and 22nd March 2014 in response to the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: In response to the 2013/14 outbreak, considerable resources were dedicated to implementing control measures, including a nationwide vector clean-up campaign between 8th and 22nd March 2014 (Break Dengue, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Break Dengue, 2014.

claim: Forty-five tonnes of tyres and twenty-five tonnes of other containers were removed during the clean-up campaign.
source: In total, forty-five tonnes of tyres and twenty-five tonnes of other containers were removed during this period.
evidence: The claim is based on reported data from the clean-up campaign.

claim: 58.6% of participants (154/263) were ELISA seropositive to at least one DENV serotype in late 2013.
source: We found that 58.6% of participants (154/263) were ELISA seropositive to at least one DENV serotype in late 2013.
evidence: The claim is supported by serological test data from the study.

claim: In October/November 2015, 74.5% (196/263) of participants were ELISA seropositive to at least one DENV serotype.
source: Two years later, in October/November 2015, this had risen to 74.5% (196/263).
evidence: The claim is supported by serological test data from the study.

claim: DENV-3 seroprevalence rose from 33.1% to 53.2% between 2013 and 2015.
source: Additional serotype-specific MIA tests confirmed that the largest rise in seroprevalence in Central Division was against DENV-3, from 33.1% to 53.2% (Table 2), consistent with the majority of RT-PCR-confirmed samples during the outbreak being of this serotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by MIA test data presented in Table 2.

claim: The majority of RT-PCR-confirmed samples during the outbreak were DENV-3.
source: Additional serotype-specific MIA tests confirmed that the largest rise in seroprevalence in Central Division was against DENV-3, from 33.1% to 53.2% (Table 2), consistent with the majority of RT-PCR-confirmed samples during the outbreak being of this serotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR testing data.

claim: Living in an urban or peri-urban environment was associated with seroconversion between 2013-15 (odds ratio 2.18 [95% CI: 0.953–5.11], p=0.068).
source: The factors most strongly associated with seroconversion between 2013–15 among initially seronegative participants were: living in an urban or peri-urban environment (odds ratio 2.18 [95% CI: 0.953–5.11], p=0.068); reporting fever in preceding two years (odds 2.94 [1.08–8.38], p=0.037); and visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years (odds 3.15 [1.06–10.10], p=0.043).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariable logistic regression analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: Reporting fever in preceding two years was associated with seroconversion between 2013-15 (odds ratio 2.94 [95% CI: 1.08–8.38], p=0.037).
source: The factors most strongly associated with seroconversion between 2013–15 among initially seronegative participants were: living in an urban or peri-urban environment (odds ratio 2.18 [95% CI: 0.953–5.11], p=0.068); reporting fever in preceding two years (odds 2.94 [1.08–8.38], p=0.037); and visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years (odds 3.15 [1.06–10.10], p=0.043).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariable logistic regression analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: Visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years was associated with seroconversion between 2013-15 (odds ratio 3.15 [95% CI: 1.06–10.10], p=0.043).
source: The factors most strongly associated with seroconversion between 2013–15 among initially seronegative participants were: living in an urban or peri-urban environment (odds ratio 2.18 [95% CI: 0.953–5.11], p=0.068); reporting fever in preceding two years (odds 2.94 [1.08–8.38], p=0.037); and visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years (odds 3.15 [1.06–10.10], p=0.043).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariable logistic regression analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: Of the participants who seroconverted, 10/38 (26.3% [13.4–43.1%]) reported visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years.
source: Of the participants who seroconverted, 10/38 (26.3% [13.4–43.1%]) reported visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years, 2/38 (5.26% [0.644–17.7%]) reported fever but did not visit a doctor, and 26/38 (68.4% [51.3–82.5%]) did not report fever (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by questionnaire data from seroconverters.

claim: Of the participants who seroconverted, 2/38 (5.26% [0.644–17.7%]) reported fever but did not visit a doctor.
source: Of the participants who seroconverted, 10/38 (26.3% [13.4–43.1%]) reported visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years, 2/38 (5.26% [0.644–17.7%]) reported fever but did not visit a doctor, and 26/38 (68.4% [51.3–82.5%]) did not report fever (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by questionnaire data from seroconverters.

claim: Of the participants who seroconverted, 26/38 (68.4% [51.3–82.5%]) did not report fever.
source: Of the participants who seroconverted, 10/38 (26.3% [13.4–43.1%]) reported visiting a doctor with fever in the preceding two years, 2/38 (5.26% [0.644–17.7%]) reported fever but did not visit a doctor, and 26/38 (68.4% [51.3–82.5%]) did not report fever (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by questionnaire data from seroconverters.

claim: The 10–19 year-old age group had the highest risk of infection during the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: Our results suggested the 10–19 year-old age group had the highest risk of infection, but we did not find strong evidence that other demographic or environmental risk factors were linked to seroconversion.
evidence: The claim is supported by age-specific seroconversion analysis.

claim: There was not strong evidence that demographic or environmental risk factors were linked to seroconversion.
source: Our results suggested the 10–19 year-old age group had the highest risk of infection, but we did not find strong evidence that other demographic or environmental risk factors were linked to seroconversion.
evidence: The claim is supported by risk factor analysis showing no significant associations.

claim: The first case was reported at Colonial War Memorial Hospital (CWM) in the week ending 4th November 2013.
source: The first case was reported at Colonial War Memorial Hospital (CWM), Fiji's largest hospital located in central urban Suva, in the week ending 4th November 2013.
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data.

claim: The outbreak took 9 weeks to reach the furthest reporting point from CWM in Central Division, a health centre 51 km away by Euclidean distance.
source: The outbreak took 9 weeks to reach the furthest reporting point from CWM in Central Division, a health centre 51 km away by Euclidean distance (i.e. as the crow flies).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial analysis of surveillance data.

claim: There was no significant association between the Euclidean distance from CWM and proportion of cluster infected.
source: However, we found no significant association between the Euclidean distance from CWM and proportion of cluster infected (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was evidence of dengue seroconversion in every cluster.
source: We did find evidence of dengue seroconversion in every cluster, however, suggesting that the outbreak eventually spread throughout Central Division.
evidence: The claim is supported by serological data from all study clusters.

claim: The model with both climate-driven variation in transmission and an additional transmission reduction performed best as measured by AIC and DIC.
source: When we jointly fitted the models to surveillance data and age-specific immunity, as measured by seropositivity to DENV-3 by MIA in 2013 and 2015, the model with both climate-driven variation in transmission and an additional transmission reduction performed best as measured by AIC and DIC (Figure 5A–B and Table 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison using AIC and DIC shown in Table 5.

claim: An estimated reduction of 57% (95% CrI: 42–82%) in transmission coincided with the clean-up campaign.
source: This additional reduction in transmission was modelled using a flexible additional sigmoidal transmission rate, and was constrained so that the midpoint of the decline occurred after the start of the campaign on 8th March 2014 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1); we estimated a reduction of 57% (95% CrI: 42–82%) in transmission that coincided with the clean-up campaign (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling fitted to surveillance and serological data.

claim: The effective reproduction number was near the critical value of one when the clean-up campaign was introduced.
source: As the effective reproduction number was near the critical value of one when the clean-up campaign was introduced (Figure 5D–E), it suggests that the main contribution of control measures may have been to bring DENV-3 infections to sufficiently low levels for transmission to cease earlier.
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The main contribution of control measures may have been to bring DENV-3 infections to sufficiently low levels for transmission to cease earlier.
source: As the effective reproduction number was near the critical value of one when the clean-up campaign was introduced (Figure 5D–E), it suggests that the main contribution of control measures may have been to bring DENV-3 infections to sufficiently low levels for transmission to cease earlier.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mathematical modeling results.

claim: 11% (1.1–39%) of infections were estimated to be reported as laboratory-tested cases.
source: Accounting for stochastic variability in weekly case reporting, we estimated that 11% (1.1–39%) of infections were reported as laboratory-tested cases and 9.3% (1.1–39%) were reported as DLI cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling fitted to surveillance data.

claim: 9.3% (1.1–39%) of infections were estimated to be reported as DLI cases.
source: Accounting for stochastic variability in weekly case reporting, we estimated that 11% (1.1–39%) of infections were reported as laboratory-tested cases and 9.3% (1.1–39%) were reported as DLI cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling fitted to surveillance data.

claim: Dengue outbreaks typically occur during the wetter, warmer season between December and July in Fiji, when vectors are most abundant.
source: In Fiji, dengue outbreaks typically occur during the wetter, warmer season between December and July, when vectors are most abundant (Goettel et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goettel et al., 1980.

claim: Between 27th October 2013 and 31st August 2014, 25,494 suspected cases of dengue were notified to the Fijian Ministry of Health.
source: Between 27th October 2013 and 31st August 2014, 25,494 suspected cases of dengue (i.e. laboratory tested or confirmed or DLI) were notified to the Fijian Ministry of Health.
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data from the Fijian Ministry of Health.

claim: 12,413 (48.7%) cases were in Central Division during the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: Of these, 12,413 (48.7%) cases were in Central Division, predominantly in the greater Suva area (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 10,679 cases were reported in the Western Division during the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: 10,679 cases were reported in the Western Division, 2048 cases were reported in the Northern division, largely in or near Labasa, the largest town of Vanua Levu island, and 354 cases were reported in the Eastern Division.
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data.

claim: 2048 cases were reported in the Northern division during the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: 10,679 cases were reported in the Western Division, 2048 cases were reported in the Northern division, largely in or near Labasa, the largest town of Vanua Levu island, and 354 cases were reported in the Eastern Division.
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data.

claim: 354 cases were reported in the Eastern Division during the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: 10,679 cases were reported in the Western Division, 2048 cases were reported in the Northern division, largely in or near Labasa, the largest town of Vanua Levu island, and 354 cases were reported in the Eastern Division.
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data.

claim: Filter paper-based surveillance conducted by ILM between December 2013 and October 2014 found 24 samples positive for DENV-3 by RT-PCR.
source: Filter paper-based surveillance conducted by ILM between December 2013 and October 2014 found 24 samples positive for DENV-3 by RT-PCR, as well as three samples positive for DENV-2 and one for DENV-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR testing data from ILM.

claim: Filter paper-based surveillance conducted by ILM between December 2013 and October 2014 found three samples positive for DENV-2 by RT-PCR.
source: Filter paper-based surveillance conducted by ILM between December 2013 and October 2014 found 24 samples positive for DENV-3 by RT-PCR, as well as three samples positive for DENV-2 and one for DENV-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR testing data from ILM.

claim: Filter paper-based surveillance conducted by ILM between December 2013 and October 2014 found one sample positive for DENV-1 by RT-PCR.
source: Filter paper-based surveillance conducted by ILM between December 2013 and October 2014 found 24 samples positive for DENV-3 by RT-PCR, as well as three samples positive for DENV-2 and one for DENV-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR testing data from ILM.

claim: During 2014/15, there was a flare up of DENV-2 in Fiji.
source: During 2014/15, there was a flare up of DENV-2 in Fiji.
evidence: The claim is based on surveillance data.

claim: Of the 543 confirmed DENV-2 cases nationally between 1st January 2015 and 29th April 2015, 437 cases (80%) were from the Northern Division.
source: However, relatively few cases occurred on Viti Levu: of the 543 confirmed cases nationally between 1st January 2015 and 29th April 2015, 437 cases (80%) were from the Northern Division (World Health Organisation, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data cited from World Health Organisation, 2015.

claim: The pre- and post-outbreak serological survey included 263 participants from the Central Division.
source: The pre- and post-outbreak serological survey included 263 participants from the Central Division, with age distribution of these participants consistent with the population distribution (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by study design and participant data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The age distribution of serosurvey participants was consistent with the population distribution.
source: The pre- and post-outbreak serological survey included 263 participants from the Central Division, with age distribution of these participants consistent with the population distribution (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pre-outbreak sera were collected as part of population representative community-based surveys of leptospirosis and typhoid conducted in Central Division between September and November 2013.
source: Pre-outbreak sera were collected as part of population representative community-based surveys of leptospirosis and typhoid conducted in Central Division between September and November 2013 (Lau et al., 2016; Watson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lau et al., 2016 and Watson et al., 2017.

claim: Post-outbreak sera were collected during a follow-up study carried out in October and November 2015.
source: Post-outbreak sera were collected during a follow-up study carried out in October and November 2015.
evidence: The claim is based on the study design.

claim: There was a noticeable right shift in the distribution of ELISA values between 2013 and 2015.
source: There was a noticeable right shift in this distribution between 2013 and 2015, with ELISA values increasing across a range of values (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A rise in ELISA value of at least three was more likely to be a genuine increase rather than measurement error.
source: The fitted model suggested that a rise in value of at least three was more likely to be a genuine increase rather than measurement error, as shown by the dashed line in Figure 2B.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mixture model fitted to the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a negative relationship between initial ELISA value and subsequent rise, with ELISA values near zero rising by around 10 units, but higher values exhibiting a smaller rise.
source: By adjusting to focus on likely infections, we found a negative relationship between initial value and subsequent rise, with ELISA values near zero rising by around 10 units, but higher values exhibiting a smaller rise (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the generalized additive model shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Individuals who reported a fever in the preceding two years had a predicted rise in ELISA value that was 2.2 (95% 0.77–3.6) units higher than those who did not (p=0.003).
source: Using a logistic model with self-reported symptoms as outcome and change in value as dependent variable, adjusting for initial value and again weighting by probability of infection, we found that individuals who reported a fever in the preceding two years had a predicted rise in ELISA value that was 2.2 (95% 0.77–3.6) units higher than those who did not (p=0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis of symptoms and ELISA values.

claim: Individuals who reported visiting a doctor with fever had a predicted ELISA value 3.3 (1.8–4.9) higher than others (p=0.0005).
source: Further, individuals who reported visiting a doctor with fever had a predicted value 3.3 (1.8–4.9) higher than others (p=0.0005).
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis of symptoms and ELISA values.

claim: There was an increase in the proportion seropositive against DENV with age in both 2013 and 2015.
source: Examining age patterns of seroprevalence, we found an increase in the proportion seropositive against DENV with age in both 2013 and 2015, and a rise in seroprevalence was observed in almost all age groups after the 2013/14 outbreak (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by age-stratified seroprevalence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A rise in seroprevalence was observed in almost all age groups after the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: Examining age patterns of seroprevalence, we found an increase in the proportion seropositive against DENV with age in both 2013 and 2015, and a rise in seroprevalence was observed in almost all age groups after the 2013/14 outbreak (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by age-stratified seroprevalence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Individuals aged 10–19 years were most likely to be infected during the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: As well as producing more precise estimates of infection risk in older groups (Table 4), this approach also suggested that individuals aged 10–19 years were most likely to be infected.
evidence: The claim is supported by age-specific infection estimates shown in Table 4.

claim: The surveillance data indicated the highest per capita level of reported disease was in the 20–29 age group.
source: This is in contrast to the surveillance data, which indicated the highest per capita level of reported disease was in the 20–29 age group (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by surveillance data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The model with only climate-driven variation in transmission could not capture the overall shape of the surveillance data.
source: As well as performing worse under AIC and DIC, the model with only climate-driven variation in transmission could not capture the overall shape of the surveillance data (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The basic model, which had neither climate-driven variation in transmission nor an additional reduction in transmission, could not jointly reproduce both surveillance and serological data.
source: The basic model, which had neither climate-driven variation in transmission nor an additional reduction in transmission, could not jointly reproduce both sets of data either (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Fitting the basic model to the surveillance data alone could reproduce the observed incidence pattern under the assumption of a simple immunising epidemic.
source: Fitting the basic model to the surveillance data alone, we could reproduce the observed incidence pattern under the assumption of a simple immunising epidemic.
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting results.

claim: The basic epidemic model underestimated the initial level of immunity and overestimated final immunity.
source: However, this basic epidemic model underestimated the initial level of immunity and overestimated final immunity.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with serological data.

claim: A similar discrepancy between serological surveys and surveillance data has been noted in previous arbovirus modelling studies for ZIKV.
source: A similar discrepancy between serological surveys and surveillance data has been noted in previous arbovirus modelling studies, albeit for ZIKV rather than DENV (Funk et al., 2016; Kucharski et al., 2016; Champagne et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Funk et al., 2016; Kucharski et al., 2016; Champagne et al., 2016.

claim: The apparent disparity between reported cases and infections estimated from the serological survey may be the result of secondary DENV infections causing more severe clinical disease.
source: The apparent disparity between reported cases and infections estimated from the serological survey may be the result of secondary DENV infections causing more severe clinical disease and therefore increasing the likelihood of seeking medical care (OhAinle et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by a citation to OhAinle et al., 2011.

claim: Fewer than 50% of individuals under age 20 had experienced DENV infection in 2013.
source: The ELISA results suggested that fewer than 50% of individuals under age 20 had experienced DENV infection in 2013 (Figure 3A), which means an infection during the 2013/14 outbreak in this group was more likely to be primary than secondary.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA seroprevalence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An infection during the 2013/14 outbreak in the under 20 age group was more likely to be primary than secondary.
source: The ELISA results suggested that fewer than 50% of individuals under age 20 had experienced DENV infection in 2013 (Figure 3A), which means an infection during the 2013/14 outbreak in this group was more likely to be primary than secondary.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from seroprevalence data.

claim: The majority of 20–29 year olds already had evidence of infection in 2013.
source: In contrast, the majority of 20–29 year olds already had evidence of infection in 2013, and hence 2013/14 outbreak would have generated relatively more secondary or tertiary infections in this group.
evidence: The claim is supported by seroprevalence data.

claim: The 2013/14 outbreak would have generated relatively more secondary or tertiary infections in the 20-29 year old group.
source: In contrast, the majority of 20–29 year olds already had evidence of infection in 2013, and hence 2013/14 outbreak would have generated relatively more secondary or tertiary infections in this group.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from seroprevalence data.

claim: Estimating population attack rates based on the proportion of seronegative individuals infected may over-estimate the true extent of infection.
source: In addition, if age-specific infection rates are indeed higher in younger groups, it means that estimating population attack rates based on the proportion of seronegative individuals infected may over-estimate the true extent of infection.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from age-specific infection patterns.

claim: Focusing on the seronegative subset of the population leads to children being over-sampled, which inflates attack rate estimates by around 10%.
source: Focusing on the seronegative subset of the population leads to children being over-sampled, which in our data inflates attack rate estimates by around 10% compared to estimates based on change in ELISA value (Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of attack rate estimation methods shown in Table 4.

claim: Spatial structure may be more important in driving transmission dynamics early in the outbreak, but might not influence the final attack rate.
source: Although the locations of health centres reporting cases in the early stages of the outbreak suggested infection spread outwards from central Suva, we found evidence of DENV infection in all study clusters. This suggests that spatial structure may be more important in driving transmission dynamics early in the outbreak, but might not influence the final attack rate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from spatial analysis of surveillance and serological data.

claim: Raw values from serological tests could potentially be used to estimate the proportion of a population who were asymptomatic during a dengue outbreak.
source: There was also a strong association between rise in ELISA value and self-reported symptoms in individuals who were likely infected, which suggests that raw values from serological tests could potentially be used to estimate the proportion of a population who were asymptomatic during a dengue outbreak, even in older age groups that were already seropositive.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the association between ELISA values and symptoms.

claim: Recall bias is a potential limitation of the risk factor analysis.
source: However, it is worth noting that the questionnaire that accompanied the serosurvey was brief and only asked about fever and visits to a doctor with fever; there may be specific factors that can better predict prior infection in such settings. We also conducted the follow up survey around 18 months after the outbreak, which means recall bias is a potential limitation of the risk factor analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: With surveillance data alone, it would not have been possible to distinguish between self-limiting outbreak driven by a decline in the susceptible population, and one that had ceased for another reason.
source: Our analysis shows the benefits of combining multiple data sources: with surveillance data alone, it would not have been possible to distinguish between self-limiting outbreak driven by a decline in the susceptible population, and one that had ceased for another reason.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Seasonal variation in transmission and herd immunity alone could not explain the fall in transmission during the 2013/14 outbreak.
source: In particular, this model suggested that seasonal variation in transmission and herd immunity alone could not explain the fall in transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results.

claim: An additional decline in transmission in March 2014, which coincided with a nationwide vector clean-up campaign, could better capture the observed patterns in serological and surveillance data.
source: However, an additional decline in transmission in March 2014, which coincided with a nationwide vector clean-up campaign, could better capture the observed patterns in serological and surveillance data.
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison results.

claim: High levels of neutralising antibodies have been shown to correlate with protection from symptomatic infection.
source: First, we assumed that seropositivity in IgG antibody tests was equivalent to protective immunity. High levels of neutralising antibodies have been shown to correlate with protection from symptomatic infection (Katzelnick et al., 2016), but it remains unclear precisely how much an individual with a given ELISA or MIA value contributes to transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Katzelnick et al., 2016.

claim: It remains unclear precisely how much an individual with a given ELISA or MIA value contributes to transmission.
source: First, we assumed that seropositivity in IgG antibody tests was equivalent to protective immunity. High levels of neutralising antibodies have been shown to correlate with protection from symptomatic infection (Katzelnick et al., 2016), but it remains unclear precisely how much an individual with a given ELISA or MIA value contributes to transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on acknowledgment of uncertainty in the field.

claim: Prior infection with one dengue serotype can lead to a cross-reactive immune response against other serotypes.
